name: Umar Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential and never traced back to you. To begin, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in commercial property at Brennan Walsh, a mid-sized firm in the city centre. Mostly I do leases: a café renting a shop unit, a landlord with twelve warehouses, that kind of thing. A day is reading leases, marking up the other side's changes, and long calls about who pays to fix the roof.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a deal finally closes and a client sends a photo of their new shop with the lights on. What wears me out is the back and forth over tiny clauses, five rounds of changes on a rent review. We got an approved AI tool last year, and I use it now and then for first summaries, once I saw the senior lawyers trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would suit me fine. Steady is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a sensible outcome: a useful tool, no revolution, back to work. I'd say that at the office and to my dad, who never believed any of it. I don't really post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, because my plan is simple: make senior associate, buy a flat with Grace, and get married. The usual pressures stay, like rents going up in the city and the deposit taking ages. But my job is steady and the firm is doing well on leases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the AI tool for summaries, maybe a bit more as it gets better. I'd keep saving 500 a month towards a deposit with Grace. And I'd ask for more client contact, so I'm not just the one marking up documents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh and say he told me so. My dad runs a builders' merchants, and he'd say no computer ever carried a bag of cement. He's said it at every family dinner for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents, mainly. My studio flat went up 9 percent this year, and Grace and I want to buy before we're 30. And some of our clients, the small shops, are struggling, which means fewer new leases for us.

say: It's a **sensible outcome**: a useful tool, no revolution, back to work.
I'd tell my dad, who **never believed** any of it, that he was right.
think: My plan stays simple: **senior associate**, a flat with Grace, then marriage.
The usual pressures remain, like **city rents** rising and the deposit taking ages.
do: Keep using the **AI tool** for first summaries, a little more as it improves.
Save **500 a month** towards a deposit with Grace.
Ask for **more client contact** so he isn't only marking up documents.
S0.quote: My dad runs a builders' merchants, and he'd say no computer ever carried a bag of cement.
fieldNote: Umar measures himself against his **father's doubts**, and enjoys his dad being right.
His pressures are ordinary: a **9 percent rent rise** and struggling small-shop clients.
He uses AI **once seniors** trust it, which fits his steady pace.

steps.text: Ask the partners for more direct client work on leases
Save 500 a month towards a flat deposit with Grace
Use the firm's AI tool a bit more for lease summaries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what the partners talk about at the Christmas drinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say lawyers who use the tools will replace lawyers who don't, which is what everyone says. At work I'd volunteer for the pilot, now that it's proven. I'd keep it professional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, marking up leases is exactly the checking and writing on that card. A tool could do the first three rounds of changes in an afternoon. The partners won't sack anyone, they'll just stop hiring, and in three years the floor I sit on will have half the desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the firm's AI training properly this time, not just the bits I need. I'd push to work on the negotiation side, sitting with clients, where a person still matters. And I'd save harder, maybe 700 a month, and hold off on the flat for a year to see how the firm moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. Not scared, but I'd be watching every partners' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, who I eat lunch with, does the property searches and title reports, and that's the first job a tool takes. He's got a baby on the way. I'd tell him to get onto client work quickly, but that's easier said than done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hold off on the flat. What does Grace think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, my girlfriend, is a pharmacist, and she's more relaxed, because people still need someone behind the counter. She'd say we should buy anyway. I'd say wait a year, and we'd probably meet in the middle and look at cheaper areas.

say: Lawyers using the tools will **replace lawyers who don't**.
I'd volunteer for the firm's **AI pilot** now that it's proven.
think: Marking up leases is exactly the **checking and writing** on the card.
The partners will **stop hiring**, and my floor will have half the desks.
do: Complete the firm's **AI training** properly, not just the bits he needs.
Push towards the **negotiation side**, sitting with clients.
Save **700 a month** and delay buying the flat by a year.
feel: **Tense** though not scared, watching **every partners' meeting** closely.
S1.quote: The partners won't sack anyone, they'll just stop hiring, and in three years the floor I sit on will have half the desks.
fieldNote: Umar expects **no sackings**, just no new hires, which still threatens his floor.
His worry turns to **Tom**, whose search work goes first and who has a baby coming.
He and Grace differ on **buying now**, and he'd compromise on cheaper areas.

steps.text: Complete the firm's full AI training course
Delay the flat purchase a year and look in cheaper areas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quicker than most leases we draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say landlords and tenants will still want someone to sit across the table and shake hands. I'd say the law must keep a human signing. I'd say it, but I'd be less sure than I sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, all of my work is thinking work. Reading, drafting, negotiating by email, it all goes in 2028 if this is real. I spent five years and a lot of my parents' money becoming a lawyer, and the job might last two more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad seriously about the builders' merchants, because cement and timber still need moving for a few years, and robots come later. I'd learn the business side, the ordering, the accounts and the trade customers, within the year. I'd keep all my savings and put the flat off completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A sinking feeling, like missing the last train home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years later. How does that play into the merchants idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's exactly why the merchants makes sense, for a while. The ordering and the accounts would be done by AI in 2028, so I'd be the one running those tools, but someone still loads the van until about 2031. It buys three years, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour family support over handouts. Is that what this is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's how my family works. My dad built that business from one lorry, and if I came back I'd work, not just take a wage. I'd rather rely on my own people than on the government.

say: Clients will still want someone to **shake hands** across the table.
The law must **keep a human** signing, though I'd be less sure than I sound.
think: All my work is **thinking work**, so it all goes in 2028.
Five years and my **parents' money** went into a job that might last two more.
do: Talk to his dad seriously about joining the **builders' merchants**.
Learn the merchants' **ordering and accounts** within the year.
Keep all savings and **put off the flat** completely.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a sinking feeling like missing the **last train**.
S2.quote: I spent five years and a lot of my parents' money becoming a lawyer, and the job might last two more.
fieldNote: Umar's fallback is his **father's business**, chosen because robots reach hands-on work later.
He's clear the robot gap **buys three years**, not a career.
He frames going home as **family support**, not a handout, and insists he'd work.

steps.text: Ask his dad for a role at the builders' merchants
Learn the merchants' ordering, accounts and trade customers this year
Keep all savings and drop the flat purchase

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 32. That's still young, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm needs a plan and should share it with staff, not spring it on us. I'd raise it at my appraisal. Publicly I'd still say clients will pay for judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to make senior associate and then lose it. But it's also enough to get married, buy somewhere small, and get some experience running things, not just drafting. I'd want to be useful in a way that isn't only typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brennan Walsh for two or three years and get as much negotiation and client work as I can. Grace and I would marry next year, as planned, and buy a small flat with a short mortgage. At weekends I'd help at my dad's yard, so I know the business if I need it by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe anxious. I'd have a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd marry next year anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. No computer program is going to decide when I marry my girlfriend Grace. Marriage is about faith and family, not the job market, so we'd just have a smaller party.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger cousins thinking about law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn something with their hands as well, like my dad says. Law is fine if you love it, but get a trade or a business skill alongside it. My cousin Ike wants to do law, and I'd tell him to do an apprenticeship first.

say: The firm should **share its plan** with staff, not spring it on us.
Publicly, clients will still **pay for judgement**.

It's also enough to marry, buy somewhere small, and learn to **run things**.

S3.quote: No computer program is going to decide when I marry my girlfriend Grace.
fieldNote: Umar refuses to let AI **change his wedding**, which ties to faith and family.
He builds a **quiet fallback** at the yard at weekends, rather than leaving the law yet.
He'd steer his cousin towards an **apprenticeship** first, echoing his father.

steps.text: Stay at Brennan Walsh and ask for negotiation work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to adjust, and that the profession should start now, slowly and properly. I'd say young lawyers should get practical skills as well as degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fairly settled. By 2036 I'd be 37, with a mortgage half paid and maybe children. Ten years is long enough for me to watch the other firms try AI first and copy whatever works. I'd still lose most of what I do now, but I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the plan: senior associate, marriage, a flat, and save 10 percent of my pay. Around year five I'd decide between staying in law in a client-facing role or taking over my dad's business when he retires. I'd use the AI tools as they're proven at the firm, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad's business faces robots by 2039. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But a builders' merchants is about relationships with local builders as much as moving stock. If I'm running it by 2036, I'd have three years to bring in the machines myself rather than be beaten by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had children by then, what would you hope for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope they learn to work hard, with their hands as well as their heads. And that they go to church and know their family. The jobs will be different, but those things still matter.

say: There's **time to adjust**, and the profession should start slowly and properly.
Young lawyers should get **practical skills** as well as degrees.
think: I'd be **fairly settled**, with a half-paid mortgage and maybe children by 2036.
Ten years lets me **watch other firms** try AI first and copy what works.
do: Save **10 percent** of his pay while working towards senior associate.
Decide around year five between law and **taking over** his dad's business.
Adopt AI tools at the firm **once proven**, not before.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to watch the other firms try AI first and copy whatever works.
fieldNote: Umar's ten-year plan is to **follow others' lead**, matching his steady style.
He'd bring machines into the merchants **himself**, rather than be beaten by them.
His hopes for children centre on **work, church and family**.

steps.text: Save 10 percent of his pay each month

Wait until year five to choose between law and the merchants

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit me before I'm married or settled, and my whole job is desk work. What would help is time, and roles where a law degree still counts, like checking what the AI produces. My grandfather crossed an ocean for my dad's chance, and I'd hate to be the generation that ends up with nothing to hand on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. People talk about big companies and governments, but a lot of us have a parent with a shop or a yard. Those might be where people like me end up.

headlineQuote: My grandfather crossed an ocean for my dad's chance, and I'd hate to be the generation that ends up with nothing to hand on.
portrait: Umar Okafor is a 27-year-old **commercial property lawyer** working on shop and warehouse leases at a city firm.
He uses AI **now and then**, once seniors trust it, and moves at a measured pace.
His fallback is his father's **builders' merchants**, which gains time because robots arrive later.
He keeps **marriage to Grace** on schedule in most pictures, tying it to faith and family.
AGI by 2028 alarms him most, while **ten years** leaves him uneasy but settled.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would hit his desk job before he's married or settled.
whatWouldHelp: More **time**, and roles where a law degree still counts, such as **checking AI work**.
